intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PRPH2 gene (179605) on chromosome 6p21.1. A digenic form of RP7 is caused by double heterozygous mutation in the PRPH2 gene and the ROM1 gene (180721).

checks.claim: Retinitis pigmentosa-7 (RP7) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the PRPH2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We report here three mutations of the human homologue of the rds gene (RDS) that cosegregate with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa in separate families.
checks.explanation: Abstract supports RDS mutations causing adRP (dominant implies heterozygous), but does not designate RP7 or explicitly state heterozygosity.

checks.claim: The PRPH2 gene is located on chromosome 6p21.1.
checks.evidence_quote: A third adRP gene in a large Irish pedigree has been mapped to chromosome 6p, showing tight linkage with the gene for peripherin
checks.explanation: The abstract places the peripherin gene on chromosome 6p. The more precise band, 6p21.1, is the standard gene location and is not given in the abstract. The instructions count adding a gene's standard location as restating the paper, so this is supported.

checks.claim: A digenic form of retinitis pigmentosa-7 is caused by double heterozygous mutation in the PRPH2 gene and the ROM1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Three families were identified with mutations in the unlinked photoreceptor-specific genes ROM1 and peripherin/RDS, in which only double heterozygotes develop retinitis pigmentosa (RP).
checks.explanation: The abstract describes digenic RP that develops only in people who are double heterozygous for mutations in peripherin/RDS (PRPH2) and ROM1. The 'RP7' label is the entry's own name for the disorder; the paper does not use it.

paragraphs.text: Retinitis pigmentosa-7 is a form of retinitis pigmentosa caused by mutation in the gene encoding peripherin/RDS (PRPH2), a photoreceptor-specific glycoprotein. It is usually transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait. Severity is often moderate, and the phenotype varies widely, even within one family. Some family members have widespread RP, while others have pericentral RP, pattern macular dystrophy, or fundus flavimaculatus. A digenic form occurs in individuals who are double heterozygotes for mutations in PRPH2 and ROM1.

checks.evidence_quote: suggests that mutant peripherin gives rise to retinitis pigmentosa
checks.explanation: The abstract implicates mutant peripherin-RDS in this form of RP.

checks.evidence_quote: A third adRP gene in a large Irish pedigree has been mapped to chromosome 6p
checks.explanation: The disease in this one pedigree is autosomal dominant. The general statement that RP7 is 'usually' dominant is not addressed.

checks.evidence_quote: The clinical severity of the disease in examined patients was moderate
checks.explanation: The abstract states that severity was moderate.

checks.evidence_quote: In some families, pericentral RP or macular dystrophy were found in family members while widespread RP was present in other members of the same families.
checks.explanation: Different phenotypes within the same family, together with 'highly variable phenotypes', support the claim.

checks.explanation: The paper mentions widespread RP, pericentral RP and macular dystrophy within families. It does not mention 'pattern' macular dystrophy or fundus flavimaculatus.

paragraphs.text: Weleber et al. (1993) described a family in which a 75-year-old woman, her 2 daughters (aged 44 and 50 years), and her 49-year-old son all carried the same peripherin/RDS deletion. The mother presented at age 63 years with a profoundly abnormal electroretinogram (ERG) and adult-onset retinitis pigmentosa. Her disease progressed dramatically over 12 years, with marked loss of peripheral visual field. One daughter developed pattern macular dystrophy at age 31 years. At age 44, her ERG was moderately abnormal, but her clinical disease was limited to the macula. The other daughter presented at age 42 years with macular degeneration and over 10 years developed the clinical picture of fundus flavimaculatus. Her peripheral visual field was preserved, but her ERG was moderately abnormal. The son had onset of macular degeneration at age 44 years. He had pericentral scotomas and a markedly abnormal ERG, and fluorescein angiography showed punctate pigment epithelial transmission defects.

checks.explanation: The ages and relationships match. The abstract says they were screened and the family has the deletion, but it does not explicitly say all four carried it.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2013) described 3 patients with early-onset retinal dystrophy who were homozygous for PRPH2 mutations, each with onset within the first year of life. Patient 1318 had Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA), with visual impairment and nystagmus. The ERG was nondetectable or reduced. A fundus photograph taken at age 29 years showed a prominent multilobulated central atrophic maculopathy surrounded by concentric rings of yellow deposits, vessel narrowing, and fine diffuse peripheral retinal changes. Patient 3256 also had LCA, with nystagmus and a nondetectable or reduced ERG. Fundus photographs taken at age 66 years showed peripheral and macular pigment deposits, choroidal sclerosis, vessel narrowing, optic disc pallor, and a central extensive atrophic maculopathy. Patient 741 had juvenile RP with a nondetectable or reduced ERG and visual acuity of 20/40. A fundus photograph at age 30 years showed diffuse retinal dystrophy with retinal vessel narrowing, retinal pigment epithelium mottling and loss, and a multilobulated maculopathy. There was also perifoveal hyperautofluorescence.

paragraphs.text: Manes et al. (2015) characterized 32 French adRP families with PRPH2 mutations. PRPH2-associated adRP was of moderate severity: 78% of eyes had visual acuity of 1-0.5, and 52% retained more than 50% of the visual field. Some patients characteristically showed vitelliform deposits or macular involvement. In some families, some members had pericentral RP or macular dystrophy while other members had widespread RP. The authors suggested that mild cases could be underdiagnosed.

paragraphs.text: Farrar et al. (1991) typed members of an Irish family with late-onset autosomal dominant RP with a series of markers from chromosome 6p. Two-point lod scores were positive with several markers, including D6S105 (Z = 6.081 at theta = 0.00) and RDS (Z = 5.376 at theta = 0.00). Multipoint analysis gave a maximum lod score of 6.6 at HLA-DRA. The authors concluded that their data provided direct evidence for an additional adRP locus. They stated that the data strongly implicated peripherin-rds, the human equivalent of the mouse retinal degeneration slow (rds) gene, as a candidate gene. Farrar et al. (1991) also reported that the 6p locus in this pedigree was tightly linked to the gene for peripherin, a photoreceptor cell-specific glycoprotein.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (2013) used targeted next-generation sequencing in a cohort of patients with LCA and juvenile RP and identified homozygous PRPH2 missense mutations in 3 patients. In patient 1318, who had LCA, they found a homozygous c.637T-C transition, resulting in a cys213-to-arg (C213R) substitution. Both parents and the patient's son were heterozygous, and an unaffected brother was homozygous wildtype. Patient 3256, who also had LCA, was homozygous for a c.554T-C transition, resulting in a leu185-to-pro (L185P) substitution. Parental DNA was not available. The same homozygous L185P mutation was found in patient 741, who had juvenile RP, and both parents were heterozygous. L185P had previously been reported in digenic RP with a ROM1 null mutation. The authors concluded that homozygous mutations in PRPH2 cause early-onset retinal dystrophy with LCA/juvenile RP phenotypes.

checks.evidence_quote: the p.L185P mutation, together with a null mutation in ROM1, has been reported to cause digenic RP.

checks.claim: Wang et al. (2013) proposed that heterozygous PRPH2 L185P carriers in digenic retinitis pigmentosa families may have a subclinical phenotype.
checks.evidence_quote: these findings suggest that, although asymptomatic, individuals harbouring the heterozygous p.L185P mutation should be expected to exhibit a subclinical phenotype

paragraphs.text: In French families with autosomal dominant RP (RP7), Manes et al. (2015) identified a recurrent novel leu254-to-gln (L254Q) mutation in the PRPH2 gene. When expressed in yeast, the mutant protein formed aggregates, suggesting abnormal folding.

checks.claim: Manes et al. (2015) identified a recurrent novel leu254-to-gln (L254Q) mutation in the PRPH2 gene in French families with autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa (RP7).
checks.evidence_quote: We showed that a new recurrent p.Leu254Gln mutation leads to protein aggregation
checks.explanation: The abstract reports the new recurrent L254Q mutation in French adRP families. 'RP7' is standard nomenclature.

checks.claim: The PRPH2 L254Q mutant protein formed aggregates when expressed in yeast.
checks.evidence_quote: Peripherin-2 protein was produced in yeast and analyzed by Western blot.
checks.explanation: The protein was expressed in yeast, and the abstract states that the L254Q mutant leads to protein aggregation.

checks.claim: Aggregation of the PRPH2 L254Q mutant protein in yeast suggested abnormal folding.
checks.evidence_quote: a new recurrent p.Leu254Gln mutation leads to protein aggregation, suggesting abnormal folding.
